meta.title: Scienteens Lab · From Mersenne to Kundt
meta.description: A physics workshop for students around age 15: historical experiments, wave propagation, musical instruments and a measurement of the speed of sound with a Kundt tube.

hero.title: The Kundt tube workshop
hero.introduction: How can we measure the speed of sound? We start with Mersenne’s cannon and echo experiments, then examine how a disturbance travels through a spring and through air. Reflection and standing waves lead us to musical instruments and, finally, to a wavelength measurement in a Kundt tube.

interview.title: From Mersenne to Kundt
interview.summary: The workshop follows five questions: how fast does sound travel, what is sound, how does a wave propagate, which standing waves fit a tube, and how can their wavelength give us the speed of sound?

facts.label: Central question
facts.value: What is sound, and how does it propagate?

steps.title: Measuring the speed of sound
paragraphs: Why do we see lightning before hearing thunder? A similar delay can be observed when a distant cannon fires: we see the flash, then hear the report. The farther away the cannon is, the longer we wait for the sound. Sound therefore takes time to travel. If we know the distance and can measure this delay, we can calculate its speed.

Marin Mersenne investigated this question in the seventeenth century, alongside his work on vibrating strings and music. In 1628, he asked a captain involved in the siege of La Rochelle to compare the flash of a cannon with the arrival of its sound. The flash marked the instant of firing, and the report marked the arrival of the sound. At these distances, the travel time of light is negligible compared with that of sound.

Let D be the distance between the cannon and the observer, and Δt the measured delay. The speed is then v = D / Δt. Obtaining these two measurements was difficult: the distance had to be known, and the delay could be short. Mersenne also used echoes and estimated elapsed time by counting his pulse. For an echo from a wall at distance D, the sound travels to the wall and back. The distance to use in the calculation is therefore 2D.

Mersenne described his investigations in Harmonie universelle, published in 1636. His measurements did not all give the same result. How accurately could he measure the distance? How accurately could he time the delay? A measured speed depends on both. We can examine his method by identifying these uncertainties and asking whether repeating the experiment would reduce them.

A Kundt tube allows us to measure the speed of sound over a much shorter distance. We will measure a wavelength and use a known frequency, rather than time a distant cannon report. To understand this method, we first need to examine what travels through the air between the source and the observer.

media.alt: Historical engraving of Mersenne and Pierre Petit looking upward beside a cannon aimed vertically.
media.title: Mersenne and Petit’s cannon experiment
media.caption: Mersenne and Pierre Petit watch a cannonball launched vertically. The engraving concerns the motion of the projectile. In sound experiments, cannon fire supplied two signals: a flash marking the firing and a report arriving after a measurable delay.

steps.title: We know its speed. What is sound?
paragraphs: We have a method for measuring the speed of sound, but what is sound? When a bell rings, what happens between the bell and our ears? The bell vibrates, yet it stays where it is. We hear it at a distance. How can its motion produce a change somewhere else in the room?

This question was already being discussed in antiquity. In De Anima, Aristotle associated the production of sound with an impact and with motion of the surrounding air. His account connects an event at the source to the air through which sound is heard. We can take up the same physical question: what happens to the air when an object vibrates, and how is this motion transmitted?

A tuning fork, a loudspeaker or a string sets the surrounding material in motion. The disturbance spreads through that material. When it reaches the ear, variations in air pressure set the eardrum in motion. A microphone responds to these pressure variations and produces an electrical signal. We can therefore identify three parts of the process: a vibrating source, a medium that transmits the disturbance, and a receiver that responds to it.

Sound travels through gases, liquids and solids. The video compares its propagation over the same distance in air, water and steel. Before watching, predict whether the arrival times will be the same, and which medium will transmit sound fastest. Compare this prediction with the observations. Since the distance is the same, a shorter arrival time corresponds to a greater speed.

Sound is a mechanical wave. Its propagation requires a material whose neighbouring regions interact, so it cannot travel through a vacuum. Other kinds of waves exist: light, for example, can travel through a vacuum. To understand mechanical propagation, we will use a spring. Its deformation and the motion of its parts are large enough to follow directly.

media.title: The speed of sound depends on the medium
media.caption: Predict the order of arrival, then compare the times in steel, water and air. The distance is the same in each case. What does the difference in arrival time tell us about the speed of sound in each material?

source.label: Aristotle, De Anima, Book II, Chapter 8

steps.title: From a pulse to a standing wave
paragraphs: A travelling wave is a disturbance that propagates from one region to another. What is disturbed depends on the system. In a spring, we can observe a displacement of the coils. In air, sound involves variations in pressure and density. In a light wave, the varying quantities include the electric field. For a mechanical wave, the disturbance spreads because neighbouring parts of the medium interact.

With a Slinky, we can follow both a compression moving along the spring and one particular coil. These motions are different. The compression can travel from one end to the other while each coil moves only near its equilibrium position. In the ideal wave model, the material oscillates locally and energy is transmitted along the spring without the material travelling with the wave.

A single movement of the hand produces a pulse. Repeating the movement regularly produces a periodic wave, for which we can measure a frequency and a wavelength. When a wave reaches an end of the spring, it is reflected. The incident and reflected waves can then overlap and produce a standing wave, with positions that remain at rest and others that oscillate.

substeps.title: A travelling pulse
substeps.text: If we briefly compress one end of a stretched Slinky, will a coil travel along the spring with the compression? Make a prediction, then give one end a short push along its length. Follow the compressed region, and repeat the experiment while watching one marked coil.

media.alt: Animation of a hand creating a longitudinal pulse in a horizontal spring.
media.title: Following a compression and a coil
media.caption: Follow the compressed region as it advances along the Slinky. Then watch one coil: it moves as the pulse passes and returns close to its initial position. The compression travels along the spring while the coils move locally.

paragraphs: The compressed region advances along the spring. The marked coil moves briefly, then returns close to its original position. As the pulse passes, neighbouring coils move closer together and then separate again. The disturbance is therefore a change in the spacing of the coils that is transmitted along the spring. A single, localised disturbance of this kind is called a pulse.

The coils move parallel to the direction in which the pulse propagates. This defines a longitudinal wave. Sound in air has the same type of motion: the air moves back and forth along the direction of propagation, producing regions that are more compressed and regions that are less compressed.

The moving coils have kinetic energy. Compressing or stretching the spring also stores elastic potential energy. As neighbouring sections act on one another, energy passes from one section to the next. The pulse can therefore transfer energy along the spring even though each section moves only around its initial position.

substeps.title: Sound propagation, wavelength and frequency
substeps.text: How does compressing one section of a spring make the next section move? The compression changes the elastic forces acting on neighbouring sections. These forces accelerate the neighbouring coils, whose movement then changes the forces on the sections farther along. The disturbance propagates through this succession of local interactions.
paragraphs: Two properties of the spring are involved. Its elasticity produces forces that oppose deformation and tend to restore the original spacing of the coils. Its sections also have mass and inertia: their velocity changes under the action of a force. The disturbance therefore takes time to spread. Its propagation speed depends on the spring and its tension; changing these can change the speed even if the hand continues to oscillate at the same frequency.

A loudspeaker produces a similar process in air. As its membrane moves forward, it compresses the air immediately in front of it. The pressure in this region rises above the surrounding pressure. The pressure difference sets neighbouring air in motion, changing the pressure and density farther away. When the membrane moves back, the nearby air expands and its pressure decreases. This region of lower pressure is called a rarefaction. Successive compressions and rarefactions propagate away from the loudspeaker.

The air has a small back-and-forth acoustic motion around its equilibrium position. It is not carried across the room with the sound. Air resists compression and has mass: its resistance to compression and its mass per unit volume both affect the propagation speed. The dots in the animation represent this collective motion in a simplified way. They do not show the random motion of individual gas molecules.

Leonhard Euler studied this transmission between neighbouring parts of a medium in work presented in 1748 and published in 1750. He considered the motion of interacting parts of an elastic medium and extended the description to many parts. A disturbance introduced in one region could then be followed as it spread through the medium. The historical question is the same as the one raised by our spring: how do local interactions produce a propagating wave?

Suppose the source now oscillates regularly. The frequency f is the number of complete oscillations per second, measured in hertz (Hz): a frequency of 100 Hz means 100 oscillations each second. The period T is the time taken for one complete oscillation, so T = 1 / f. The wavelength λ is the distance between successive points at the same stage of the oscillation, such as two neighbouring compressions or two neighbouring rarefactions.

During one period T, the wave advances by one wavelength λ. Using distance = speed × time, we obtain λ = vT. Since T = 1 / f, this becomes v = fλ. We can thus determine the propagation speed from two measurements: the number of oscillations per second and the distance over which one complete spatial repetition extends.

For sound in air under the same conditions, the speed is approximately independent of frequency over the audible range. If the source oscillates twice as often, successive compressions are separated by half the distance: the wavelength is halved. For a rounded speed of 340 m/s, a frequency of 100 Hz gives a wavelength of 3.4 m, while 200 Hz gives 1.7 m. In the Kundt tube, we will use the relation in the other direction: measure λ at a known f to find v.

source.label: François Baskevitch, Calculer la vitesse du son après Newton : le défi du jeune Euler, p. 45

media.alt: Animation of a loudspeaker producing successive compressions in air molecules.
media.title: A periodic disturbance in air
media.caption: Watch the motion of the dots near the source, then follow a compression as it moves away. The dots oscillate locally while the compression propagates. One wavelength is the distance between two successive compressions.

media.alt: Animation comparing several periodic patterns with different spatial repetitions.
media.title: Different wavelengths in the same medium
media.caption: Compare how many complete repetitions fit into the same distance. More repetitions correspond to a shorter wavelength. At the same propagation speed, v = fλ, so the shorter wavelength corresponds to the higher frequency.

substeps.title: Transverse waves and their graphs
substeps.text: Now move one end of the Slinky from side to side, perpendicular to its length. The coils move perpendicular to the direction in which the disturbance propagates. This defines a transverse wave. The motion of a vibrating guitar string is another example.

media.alt: Diagram comparing compressions in a longitudinal wave with the sinusoidal representation of a transverse wave.
media.title: Longitudinal and transverse waves
media.caption: Particles oscillate parallel to propagation in a longitudinal wave and perpendicular to it in a transverse wave. Both descriptions use the same wavelength, frequency and propagation speed.

media.alt: Diagram showing wavelength measured horizontally between two equivalent points of a transverse wave.
media.title: Measuring wavelength on a transverse wave
media.caption: Measure horizontally from one crest to the next, or between other consecutive points in the same phase. This distance is one wavelength. The particles oscillate vertically while the pattern propagates horizontally.

paragraphs: On a snapshot of the spring, a crest is a point of maximum displacement to one side of equilibrium, and a trough is a point of maximum displacement to the other side. The amplitude is the greatest displacement from equilibrium. Measure the wavelength along the spring between two consecutive crests or two consecutive troughs. These are equivalent points of the repeating pattern.

We can also follow one coil over time and record its displacement. This gives a different graph. A graph of displacement against position shows how the spring is deformed at one instant; it gives the wavelength. A graph of displacement against time shows how one coil oscillates; it gives the period. Always check the horizontal axis before deciding which quantity can be measured.

A sinusoidal curve can represent a sound wave too, but sound in air remains longitudinal. If the graph shows pressure against position, the height of the curve represents a pressure variation. It is not the path followed by the air. A maximum on this graph corresponds to a compression and a minimum to a rarefaction; the air moves back and forth along the direction of propagation.

Frequency and amplitude describe different properties. A higher frequency usually corresponds to a higher perceived pitch. A larger sound-pressure amplitude generally corresponds to a louder sound. On a microphone recording, the time between repetitions gives the period and hence the frequency, while the size of the recorded variation is related to the sound-pressure amplitude.

substeps.title: Reflection, superposition and standing modes
substeps.text: What happens to a crest when a transverse pulse reaches a fixed end? Make a prediction, then send a pulse along the Slinky and observe its return. At the fixed end, the total displacement must remain zero. The incident and reflected displacements cancel there, so the reflected pulse is inverted: a crest returns as a trough.
paragraphs: When two pulses overlap, their displacements add at each position. Displacements in the same direction reinforce one another. Displacements in opposite directions partly or completely cancel. For small disturbances, the pulses continue propagating after the overlap. This is the principle of superposition, which applies to both isolated pulses and periodic waves.

If the source oscillates continuously, the incident wave overlaps with its reflection. Two waves of the same frequency and wavelength, with equal amplitudes and travelling in opposite directions, produce an ideal standing wave. The combined pattern no longer advances along the spring. Some positions stay at rest while the sections between them continue to oscillate.

A displacement node is a position where the displacement remains zero throughout the cycle. A displacement antinode is a position where the oscillation amplitude is greatest. Between two neighbouring nodes, the section of spring moves first to one side of equilibrium, then to the other. The next section, on the other side of a node, moves in the opposite direction.

The distance between two neighbouring nodes is λ / 2. A node and its nearest antinode are separated by λ / 4. To identify a node, follow the point over a complete cycle: it must remain at equilibrium at every instant. A point that crosses equilibrium briefly can still be oscillating and is not necessarily a node.

Vary the frequency of the source. At certain frequencies, the amplitude becomes much larger. The source is then driving the spring close to one of its natural frequencies: this is resonance. The allowed standing modes depend on the length, the propagation speed and the constraints at the ends. A mode must satisfy these end conditions, which determines the wavelengths and frequencies that fit the system.

In a real spring or tube, damping dissipates energy, so the source must continue supplying energy to maintain the oscillation. The resonance does not produce an indefinitely growing amplitude. It produces a strong response that makes the spatial pattern easier to observe. Once the pattern is established, the spacing between its nodes allows us to measure the wavelength.

substeps.title: Standing waves on a guitar string
substeps.text: Pluck an open guitar string, then press it against the twelfth fret and pluck it again. Before listening, predict what will happen to the note. The same string is used in both cases, but pressing it against a fret changes the length of the part that can vibrate. Giancoli’s illustration shows these two situations: the whole string in (a), then a shorter vibrating section in (b).
paragraphs: When the string is pulled sideways and released, its tension produces a restoring force. The displaced section starts moving back towards equilibrium and sets neighbouring sections in motion. Transverse waves travel along the string and reflect at its supports. For a small vibration, we can treat the string as flexible, uniformly stretched and fixed at both ends of its vibrating length.

For an open string, this length L extends from the nut, the small support near the head of the guitar, to the bridge on its body. Neither support allows appreciable transverse motion, so the two ends are approximately displacement nodes. In the simplest standing mode, the section between them oscillates with one antinode at its centre. One half-wavelength fits into L: the fundamental wavelength is therefore λ₁ = 2L.

The fundamental is the lowest natural frequency of the string. Using v = fλ gives f₁ = vₛ / (2L), where vₛ is the propagation speed along the string. It is not the speed of sound in the surrounding air. Higher modes fit two, three or more half-wavelengths into the same length. In this ideal model, their frequencies are 2f₁, 3f₁ and so on. These integer multiples of the fundamental are called harmonics.

Pressing the string firmly against a fret creates a new support. The section that mainly vibrates now extends from that fret to the bridge. Its length is shorter, while its tension and mass per unit length remain approximately unchanged. The propagation speed is consequently almost the same. A shorter wavelength must then correspond to a higher frequency. At the twelfth fret, the vibrating length is half the open-string length: the fundamental frequency doubles and the note rises by one octave.

For example, consider a vibrating length of 0.65 m and a wave speed of 143 m/s along the string. The fundamental wavelength is 1.30 m and the frequency is 143 / 1.30 = 110 Hz. Shortening the vibrating length to 0.325 m gives a wavelength of 0.65 m and a frequency of 220 Hz. Each point of the string now completes twice as many oscillations per second.

The tuning peg changes the note in another way. Tightening the string increases its tension and the propagation speed, so its natural frequencies rise even if L stays the same. The mass per unit length matters too. A heavier string has more inertia for the same tension, giving a lower wave speed and lower frequencies. This explains why guitar strings of approximately equal vibrating length can produce different notes.

A plucked string usually vibrates in several modes at once. How strongly each mode is excited depends, among other things, on where and how the string is plucked. Try plucking near the bridge and then nearer the centre. The note can keep the same fundamental frequency while its tone changes because the relative amplitudes of the harmonics differ.

The bridge transmits the string’s vibration to the soundboard. The larger vibrating surface moves the surrounding air much more effectively than the thin string alone. The outgoing sound consists of longitudinal pressure disturbances in air, whereas the string’s motion is transverse. Their frequencies correspond, but their propagation speeds and wavelengths are different. The string and the Kundt tube therefore share standing-wave patterns, even though the material that oscillates and the direction of its motion are different.

media.alt: Giancoli’s guitar illustration: (a) an open string with a fundamental standing-wave pattern; (b) a finger presses a fret, shortening the vibrating section between the fret and bridge.
media.title: An open string and a fingered string
media.caption: In (a), the string vibrates from the nut to the bridge. In (b), the fret becomes one end of the shorter vibrating section. Only one string and its fundamental mode are represented. The paired curves show the string at opposite extremes of its oscillation.

steps.title: From Chladni figures to a closed tube
paragraphs: How can we observe the pattern of a vibration when the motion itself is difficult to follow? Ernst Chladni used sand on vibrating plates and published his investigations in 1787. Drawing a bow along an edge set the plate in motion. The grains moved over its surface and formed patterns that changed with the mode of vibration.

The strongly vibrating regions disturb the sand, which tends to collect along nodal lines where the plate moves very little. A Chladni figure therefore marks positions of small displacement. Changing the excitation or the constraints changes the mode and the pattern. The plate vibrates in two dimensions. We will examine an air column in a narrow tube, where we can follow the variation mainly along one direction.

Consider an ideal tube of length L with two rigid, closed ends. Air cannot move through either wall, so there is a displacement node at each end. In the lowest non-zero mode, the distance between these end nodes is half a wavelength: L = λ₁ / 2. The next modes fit two, three and more half-wavelengths into the same length. Writing n for this number gives L = nλₙ / 2, hence λₙ = 2L / n.

From v = fλ, we obtain fₙ = nv / (2L), with n = 1, 2, 3, … . The fundamental frequency is f₁ = v / (2L), and the next resonant frequencies are its integer multiples. Before substituting numbers, predict what happens to the fundamental when the length is doubled. Then use the expression to check the prediction and calculate the change.

What does a node refer to in a sound wave? At a closed end, the air displacement is zero, but the pressure-oscillation amplitude is large. This position is a displacement node and a pressure antinode. Conversely, a displacement antinode corresponds to a pressure node in the ideal acoustic standing wave. The positions of the nodes therefore depend on whether we represent displacement or pressure.

A microphone responds to pressure variations. A large signal marks a pressure antinode, which a displacement diagram represents as a node. This lets us compare the microphone measurements with the diagrams without confusing the two quantities. In our apparatus, the loudspeaker drives a moving boundary. The two-rigid-end model is an approximation, and its predicted frequencies must be compared with the measured resonances.

media.alt: Historical line drawing of a vibrating plate sprinkled with sand and excited with a bow.
media.title: Making nodal lines visible
media.caption: The sand tends to leave the strongly vibrating regions and collect along nodal lines. The pattern marks positions where the plate moves very little. Changing the mode changes these lines and produces a different figure.

source.label: E. F. F. Chladni, Entdeckungen über die Theorie des Klanges (1787)

steps.title: Kundt’s tube: measuring a wavelength
paragraphs: In 1866, August Kundt published a method for producing acoustic dust figures inside a tube and using them to determine the speed of sound in gases and solids. In his apparatus, a vibrating rod excited the gas in the tube. The gas motion rearranged a light powder, producing a repeated pattern along the tube. The spacing of this pattern could be measured to find the wavelength.

In our apparatus, a loudspeaker supplies a frequency that can be set, and a microphone measures the pressure variation at different positions along the tube. Vary the frequency slowly to find a strong response, then examine the signal along the tube. For the mode being studied, predict where pressure nodes and antinodes should occur and compare these positions with the measurements.

Let d be the distance between equivalent neighbouring positions. Two adjacent displacement nodes are separated by λ / 2. Two adjacent pressure nodes have the same spacing, as do two adjacent pressure antinodes. A pressure antinode is a position where the pressure-oscillation amplitude is greatest. Take care to compare the same kind of position: a pressure node and its nearest pressure antinode are only λ / 4 apart.

In the elementary interpretation of a dust figure, the spacing between the main repeated deposits gives half a wavelength. The grains do not directly trace the displacement of the air: their motion also depends on acoustic forces and air circulation. The powder reveals a repeated spatial pattern, whose spacing can be checked independently with the microphone.

Measure across several intervals to reduce the effect of uncertainty in locating a single position. Suppose the distance from the first chosen pressure antinode to the sixth is 0.85 m. Six positions enclose five intervals, so d = 0.85 / 5 = 0.17 m. Since d = λ / 2, the wavelength is λ = 2d = 0.34 m. Count the intervals before dividing the measured distance.

With the driving frequency known, we can calculate v = fλ. For example, f = 1000 Hz and λ = 0.34 m give v = 340 m/s. For the experiment, use the actual frequency and measured distances. Repeat the measurement and compare the speeds obtained from different modes. Uncertainty in locating the pressure antinodes produces uncertainty in λ and therefore in v.

Record the air temperature too, since the speed of sound in air depends on temperature. If the result differs from a reference value, examine the measurements and assumptions. Were equivalent positions compared? Was the frequency stable? How accurately were distances measured? Did the assumed end conditions describe the apparatus? These checks help us assess the result before attributing the difference to the gas itself.

We can repeat the experiment with a different gas. At the same driving frequency, a change in wavelength means a change in propagation speed. Mersenne estimated the speed from a distance and a travel time. Kundt’s method uses a wavelength and a frequency. Both determine how quickly a disturbance propagates, using quantities that their apparatus allows us to measure.

source.label: August Kundt, On a New Kind of Acoustic Dust Figures (1866)

game.title: The Resonance Lab
game.description: Choose a tube and identify its end conditions. Predict how changing its length or the driving frequency will affect the resonance, then test the change. Compare the modes to find which wavelengths fit the tube and how the resonant frequencies are related.

other.title: Supporting material
other.description: I use Serway, Cutnell and Johnson, and Giancoli when preparing my physics courses. The notes below contain definitions, diagrams, worked examples and exercises on wave properties and musical instruments. In this workshop, the historical experiments give us the starting questions. We then follow the physical explanation and the calculations needed to interpret our own measurements.
